content.title: About
content.content: Chicken is a widely consumed source of protein obtained from domestic poultry. It is commonly used as fillet, breast, thigh, or whole carcass. Grilled with sauce, it stays juicy and develops a flavorful crust.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken is the most consumed meat worldwide.
Its low fat content makes it a staple in weight‑loss diets.
Grilling helps retain more B‑vitamins compared with deep‑frying.
Yogurt, lemon, or soy‑based sauces are popular marinades before grilling.
Chicken bones are rich in collagen, beneficial for joints and skin.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken provides all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Especially skin‑less breast, making it suitable for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains niacin, vitamin B6 and B12, supporting metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides phosphorus, selenium and zinc, important for bones, immunity and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Satiety support
items.content: High protein content promotes lasting fullness.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked chicken may harbor salmonella; cook to an internal temperature of 75 °C.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken protein.

items.title: Sodium in sauces
items.content: Prepared sauces can be high in salt; monitor sodium intake if needed.

items.title: Skin content
items.content: Chicken skin contains more fat and should be eaten in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chicken can be served sliced, added to salads, wraps, pasta, or used in stews. Grilled with sauce, it works well as a main dish or in sandwiches.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh raw chicken refrigerated at +2‑4 °C for up to 2 days. Store cooked chicken in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days or freeze for up to 3 months.

chicken-or-turkey-potatoes-corn-and-chee.title: Chicken or Turkey with Potatoes, Corn and Cheese, with Gravy

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of pieces of chicken or turkey baked together with potatoes, corn and cheese, served under a savory meat gravy. This combination provides a balanced mix of protein, carbohydrates and fats, making the meal hearty and flavorful.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken and turkey belong to the same family of birds – the pheasants, but turkey contains slightly more iron.
Potatoes are one of the world’s most popular root vegetables, and their nutritional value depends on the cooking method.
Corn is rich in antioxidant carotenoids that give it a yellow color.
Grated cheese melts and forms a fragrant crust, locking moisture inside the dish.
Gravy is traditionally made from browned meat drippings, broth and flour, giving it a thick texture.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken and turkey provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Poultry meat and potatoes supply vitamins B6 and B12, supporting the nervous system and metabolism.

items.title: Fiber and potassium from corn
items.content: Corn adds dietary fiber and potassium, which help maintain healthy blood pressure.

items.title: Calcium and phosphorus from cheese
items.content: Cheese is a good source of calcium and phosphorus, important for bone and tooth health.

items.title: Energy density
items.content: The mix of carbs (potatoes, corn) and fats (cheese, gravy) provides sustained satiety.

items.title: Dairy allergy or lactose intolerance
items.content: Cheese and gravy may trigger reactions in people sensitive to milk proteins.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Prepared gravy and cheese often contain a lot of salt; those with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: The dish can be calorie‑dense because of cheese and gravy; moderate consumption is advised for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Thorough cooking required
items.content: Chicken and turkey must be fully cooked to avoid the risk of salmonella.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, cutting it into individual portions. Garnish with fresh herbs, sour cream or hot sauce if desired. It pairs well with a light salad or vegetable side.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool leftovers to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat thoroughly until steaming hot.

content.title: About
content.content: Chow mein noodles are thin egg noodles traditionally used in the Chinese stir‑fried dish “chow mein”. They are made from wheat flour, eggs, water and salt, boiled to al dente and quickly fried with vegetables, meat or seafood. The noodles have a firm, springy texture and a slightly sweet flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chow mein originates from Jiangsu province, where the noodles were traditionally served stir‑fried with soy sauce.
Traditional egg noodles contain about 8 % egg, giving them a characteristic yellow hue.
In China, chow‑mein noodles are often handmade “home‑style”, but most countries use dried instant noodles as a substitute.
The dish became popular in the United States in the 1970s thanks to Chinese restaurants on the West Coast.
Noodles can be thin or medium thickness; thickness affects cooking time and mouthfeel.

items.title: Carbohydrate source
items.content: Noodles provide a quick source of energy due to their high complex‑carbohydrate content.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Egg noodles deliver about 12 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: They contain thiamine, niacin and folate, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Noodles supply iron, magnesium and phosphorus, beneficial for blood formation and bone health.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: When prepared without excess oil, the dish remains relatively low‑fat.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Wheat‑based noodles contain gluten and are unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce and seasonings can make the dish high in sodium, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: While the noodles themselves are low‑fat, stir‑frying with a lot of oil increases calories.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Egg noodles may trigger reactions in individuals allergic to eggs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Boil the noodles in salted water for 3–5 minutes until al dente, then quickly stir‑fry over high heat with vegetables (carrot, cabbage, onion), meat or seafood. Add soy sauce, oyster sauce and a small amount of oil. Serve hot, optionally garnished with sliced green onions.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry noodles in an airtight container in a cool, dry place for up to 12 months. After cooking, cool the noodles, transfer to a container and refrigerate for no more than 3 days. When reheating, add a little oil to restore their springiness.

content.title: About
content.content: Regular or quick oatmeal prepared with non‑dairy milk (soy, almond, oat, etc.) and added fat is a nutritious breakfast rich in complex carbs, fiber, and healthy fats, providing lasting satiety.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oats have been cultivated for over 5,000 years.
Quick‑cooking oats are pre‑steamed and cut thinner for faster preparation.
Using plant‑based milk makes the dish vegan and lactose‑free.
Adding fat (oil, coconut oil, nut butter) enhances absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.
Oats contain beta‑glucan, a soluble fiber that helps lower cholesterol.

items.title: Rich in beta‑glucan
items.content: Beta‑glucan helps regulate blood sugar and supports heart health.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Provides steady energy release and prolonged fullness.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Oatmeal supplies thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6, essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Beneficial fats when oil is added
items.content: Plant oils add omega‑3 and omega‑6 fatty acids, supporting brain function and skin health.

items.title: Gluten sensitivity
items.content: Oats may contain trace gluten; those with celiac disease should choose certified gluten‑free oats.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce mineral absorption; soaking or fermenting lowers its level.

items.title: Calorie density with added fat
items.content: Adding oil increases calories, so portion size should be monitored.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Combine oats with non‑dairy milk, a pinch of salt, and a small amount of oil; bring to a boil or microwave. Top with fruit, nuts, seeds, or spices such as cinnamon or vanilla.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry oats in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked oatmeal can be kept in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Stewed rice, Puerto Rican style is a traditional Puerto Rican dish made with long‑grain rice, tomato‑based sauce, aromatic spices, and often beans, meat or seafood. The rice cooks in a small amount of liquid, becoming tender and infused with flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish is typically prepared in a single pot, simplifying cooking and preserving aromas.
Traditional recipes use "adobo" – a blend of soy sauce, garlic and spices that gives the characteristic taste.
In Puerto Rico rice is a symbol of abundance and is frequently served at celebrations.
Variations may include chicken, pork, chorizo sausage, or seafood such as shrimp and mussels.
Stewed rice is often accompanied by fried plantains or sliced avocado.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Rice provides sustained energy release, helping maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in fiber when beans are added
items.content: Legumes increase dietary fiber content, supporting digestive health.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: The dish supplies thiamine, niacin and folate, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: When prepared with minimal oil, the meal remains light and suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Antioxidants from tomatoes and spices
items.content: Lycopene and other phytochemicals help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared with store‑bought adobo sauce the dish can be high in salt; adjust seasoning as needed.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: Versions containing shrimp or mussels may trigger reactions in people allergic to shellfish.

items.title: Gluten (if soy sauce contains wheat)
items.content: Traditional adobo may include wheat‑based soy sauce; choose a gluten‑free alternative when required.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve stewed rice hot as a main course or side. Pair it with fried plantains, avocado, fresh salsa, or a green salad. A squeeze of lime adds a bright citrus note.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the dish to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat on the stovetop or in the microwave, adding a splash of water to restore moisture.
